LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning
for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels

 

Zixi Zhang 1  Jiayi Nie 2  Haoran Wu 2 3  Yujie Yan 4  Yann Herklotz 5  Rika Antonova 2  Robert Mullins 2  Yiren Zhao 1  George A. Constantinides 1  Jianyi Cheng 4 

††footnotetext: 1Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom 2Department of Computer Science and Technology, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom 3Quettaflop AI 4School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom 5Computer Science Department, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland. Correspondence to: George A. Constantinides <g.constantinides@imperial.ac.uk>, Jianyi Cheng <jianyi.cheng@ed.ac.uk>.
Preprint.
Abstract

Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time, instead of checking every single line of generated code. LARK formalizes the GPU machine model and the semantics of each operation in Lean 4 once per target language, and the Lean 4 semantics of any incoming kernel is derived from these pre-built definitions. LLM agents then automate the proof in two steps. First, an agent decomposes the whole kernel semantics into smaller segments and Lean 4 verifies this segmentation, which addresses the intractability of proving equivalence for large kernels directly. Second, agents write Lean proofs that each kernel segment matches its high-level PyTorch counterpart. Together, the two steps give whole-program equivalence. We demonstrate that LARK can be used 1) to ensure correctness in existing code-generation agents and 2) to automatically verify human-written kernel libraries. On the KernelCraft GPU tasks, combined with a simple ReAct agent, LARK enables GLM 5.3 to fully verify 10 of 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all 5 Level-2 kernels. Moreover, over 10 production kernels randomly sampled from popular open-source LLM serving frameworks, LARK verifies 9 and identifies a new data race bug in the tenth. We believe LARK represents a significant step toward verifiable code generation in the agentic era.

1 Introduction

GPU kernels are where the cost of training and serving deep learning models is paid, and the fastest are hand-scheduled CUDA, PTX, or HIP written close to the metal (Wu et al., 2026; Dao et al., 2022; Tillet et al., 2019). Such code is increasingly written by LLM agents (Nie et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2025; Beel et al., 2025; Baronio et al., 2026), and a plausible kernel is not a correct one: the same models that write fluent code write fluent bugs (Lange et al., 2025; Chatterjee et al., 2026). Every regenerated kernel needs its own correctness check, at the pace of generation. Existing checks fall short on one count or the other (Figure 1, top). Tests on sampled inputs keep pace but give evidence, never a guarantee; human review reasons about all inputs but cannot keep pace; an LLM judge removes the human but not the problem. What a generated kernel needs is a proof of a precise equivalence statement, checked by a proof assistant such as Lean 4 (Moura and Ullrich, 2021), and formal tools do not provide one either: GPUVerify (Betts et al., 2012) proves race and divergence freedom, not the specification; a verified compiler (Leroy, 2009) certifies its own translation, not a generated kernel; a hand-written model (Armstrong et al., 2019) or proof (Klein et al., 2010) puts a human back where we want automation.

We present LARK (Lean-Assisted Reasoning for Kernels), an agentic framework in which LLM agents write both the model of the kernel and the proof, and Lean checks both. Once per target language, LARK formalizes in Lean a machine model of the GPU and the semantics of each operation and measures them against the hardware; the machine model is shared across languages, so a new target supplies only its operations and their semantics, and we instantiate LARK for PTX, CUDA, and AMD HIP. Given a PyTorch specification and a kernel from any generator, the kernel’s semantics is derived from these pinned parts, agents write the proofs, and Lean checks every step, so a wrong agent output is a failed proof, never a wrong theorem. This division of labor raises three challenges:

1) Semantic gap. The kernel’s Lean semantics is spelled out operation by operation over the machine model, while the PyTorch reference has a tensor-level semantics in Lean. LARK bridges the two by deriving a flat model of the kernel and having an LLM agent segment it, verifiably, into a segment-level model that a proof can induct on (Section 4.2).

2) Fidelity versus tractability. The machine model must be sound for the hardware yet abstract enough to prove against. LARK’s model computes over exact numbers, runs a phase’s threads in sequence, and treats undefined behavior as a fault; what makes this sound, race freedom above all, is proved in Lean per kernel as obligations, and a kernel that can fault or race has no theorem (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

3) Trust boundaries. Any assumption the theorem depends on but Lean does not verify must be trusted by humans; we call this set the trust boundary. LARK keeps it small and fixed by the task, the hardware machine model, the fixed mapping from operation semantics to kernel semantics, and the formalized task specification, so it can be reviewed once in advance; every run produces a Lean certificate that any Lean project re-checks without repeating the LARK procedure (Section 4.3).

LARK tackles these three challenges, and we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present LARK, an agentic formal-verification workflow for GPU kernels in low-level, close-to-metal languages. To our knowledge, LARK is the first attempt at using agents to produce formally verified low-level GPU code for equivalence check.

  • •

    We show how to formalize low-level GPU semantics in Lean 4 and prove functional equivalence between a GPU kernel and a PyTorch reference. LARK combines verified program segmentation with iterative agentic proof construction, and humans review the task’s trust boundary only once, ahead of time in dependent of kernel inputs; every kernel generated afterwards is certified relative to those trusted assumptions.

  • •

    We demonstrate that LARK can be integrated with agentic code-generation harnesses to certify their kernels and serves as an automated verifier for human-written kernels. On KernelCraft, GLM 5.3 certifies 10 of the 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all five fused Level-2 kernels, every semantics-breaking mutant is rejected, and nine of ten production kernels verify while the tenth is rejected for a real data race (Section 5).

2 Motivating Example

Figure 2 makes the three challenges of Section 1 concrete. The specification (Figure 2(a)) multiplies two FP16 matrices. The kernel (Figure 2(c)) is LLM-written PTX, the virtual instruction set CUDA compiles to, in the shape of fast kernels: each one-warp block computes one output tile (line 3), staging slabs of AA and BB into shared memory (lines 5–7) and multiplying them on the tensor cores (lines 8–11) before storing the tile (lines 16–17). The theorem (Figure 2(b)) relates the two through the state of a machine that runs the kernel, under a premise of the task, not of the kernel; a test samples it, a proof establishes it for every input (Section 3).

What a guarantee catches. Line 13 of Figure 2(c) is a one-line bug a generator could write: without the barrier, a lane may overwrite a staged slab another lane is still reading. Nothing marks the omission among 300 lines that look alike, and the kernel can pass every test, since on a given GPU the warp may finish ldmatrix before any lane stores, while PTX promises no such order. LARK catches it in Lean: the race-freedom obligation it proves before any value (Section 4.2) fails for line 13 with a counterexample, two lanes meeting at one shared cell, that points to where the barrier belongs; with line 15 the kernel gets the theorem in Figure 2(b).

Where the challenges show. Semantic gap: the conclusion speaks of the matrix A​BAB, while the kernel updates four registers per lane per mma (line 10) and loops by a branch to a label (line 15), naming no tile, iteration, or sum to induct on. Fidelity versus tractability: a model faithful to every interleaving of 32 lanes and 32 blocks admits no tractable proof, and each abstraction that helps has a condition, such as sequential threads needing lines 6 and 8 never to race, that must be proved rather than assumed for the theorem to be worth anything. Trust: that the Lean mma is what the tensor core computes, that bar.sync is a barrier, and that the Lean specification and interface are those of the task can only be believed, so this trust boundary (Section 1) must exclude whatever an agent writes and stay a short, fixed list; Section 4 shows how LARK meets each challenge.

3 Problem Definition

Section 2 showed the theorem informally; we now state, for a fixed target language, what is proved, what is assumed, and what a verifier must deliver.

Specification. A specification SS is a Torch module, denoting a total function ⟦S⟧:D→T\llbracket S\rrbracket:D\to T from the inputs DD with the declared shapes, types, and constraints to the output tensors TT. SS is the ground truth.

Kernel and machine model. A kernel KK is a program in the target language with a launch geometry. Its meaning is fixed only relative to a machine model MM: the states ΣM\Sigma_{M}, a partial semantics for each operation, a scheduling rule, and a representation of values (ours is in Section 4.1). These define the partial whole-launch semantics ⟦K⟧M:ΣM⇀ΣM\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}:\Sigma_{M}\rightharpoonup\Sigma_{M}, defined at σ\sigma when every maximal execution from σ\sigma is finite, fault-free, and ends in the same state.

Interface. Tensors enter and leave the machine through memory under the task’s interface II: the region and layout of each tensor, the launch geometry, and the disjointness of the regions. II belongs to the task, not to KK, and yields a precondition InI​(σ,x)\mathrm{In}_{I}(\sigma,x), true when σ\sigma has the declared geometry and holds x∈Dx\in D in the declared regions, and an output extractor OutI:ΣM→T\mathrm{Out}_{I}:\Sigma_{M}\to T. In Figure 2(b), StdPre is InI\mathrm{In}_{I}, stdExtract is OutI\mathrm{Out}_{I}, and runLaunch is ⟦K⟧M\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}.

Equivalence. Both sides are compared as real-valued tensors, the kernel’s operations read over exact reals (Sections 4.1 and 4.3). KK is equivalent to SS under MM and II, written K≡M,ISK\equiv_{M,I}S, if

∀x∈D.∀σ∈ΣM.InI​(σ,x)\displaystyle\forall x\in D.\;\forall\sigma\in\Sigma_{M}.\quad\mathrm{In}_{I}(\sigma,x) (1)
⟹⟦K⟧M​(σ)↓∧OutI​(⟦K⟧M​(σ))=⟦S⟧​(x).\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\;\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma){\downarrow}\;\wedge\;\mathrm{Out}_{I}\big(\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma)\big)=\llbracket S\rrbracket(x).

Quantifying over every initial state that holds the input forbids KK from depending on memory outside the interface, and reading the output from the declared region fixes where the result lands. This is all that equivalence in memory behavior means: the memories of MM are unbounded (Section 4.1), so a write outside the interface is invisible to the statement, and out-of-bounds safety on the host’s allocations is not guaranteed.

Trust boundary. A proof of Equation 1 is a proof about MM; to carry over to the real hardware and host ℋ\mathcal{H}, it needs facts no proof inside MM can establish: that MM is faithful to the hardware up to its idealizations, that the formalization of SS denotes ⟦S⟧\llbracket S\rrbracket, and that the host honors II. This trust boundary must be fixed by the task, not by the kernel: MM and II are unavoidably premises, nothing else may be, and properties of KK such as race freedom or termination are obligations, proved per kernel (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

Problem definition. Fix a target language with machine model MM. Given a specification SS, an interface II, and a kernel KK, produce either a certificate (Π,π)(\Pi,\pi) or a rejection, which makes no claim about KK. The premises Π=ΠM∪ΠK\Pi=\Pi_{M}\cup\Pi_{K} are ΠM\Pi_{M}, the faithfulness of MM to ℋ\mathcal{H}, and ΠK\Pi_{K}, the task’s signature and launch, from which InI\mathrm{In}_{I} and OutI\mathrm{Out}_{I} are computed by fixed definitions; both are reported with the result (Section 4.3). The machine-checked proof π\pi establishes

ΠK⊢K≡M,IS,\Pi_{K}\;\vdash\;K\equiv_{M,I}S,

with InI\mathrm{In}_{I} satisfiable for every input in DD, and hence ΠM⊧K≡ℋ,IS\Pi_{M}\models K\equiv_{\mathcal{H},I}S: π\pi supplies the equivalence in MM, ΠM\Pi_{M} the passage from MM to ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Requirements. A solution must be sound: a certificate is issued only if K≡M,ISK\equiv_{M,I}S holds, and π\pi is checked by a checker that does not trust its producer. Soundness makes both conjuncts of Equation 1 obligations, proved rather than assumed. Among sound solutions we prefer the more complete, certifying more of the kernels that are equivalent, and the more trustworthy, certifying with a smaller ΠM\Pi_{M}. The second objective separates this problem from classical equivalence checking: race freedom and the other regularities that make GPU kernels tractable are properties of KK, proved per kernel, so that ΠM\Pi_{M} keeps only what no per-kernel proof can discharge.

4 Method

Section 3 asks for a certificate whose premises say nothing about the kernel: everything inside the trust boundary must be fixed before the kernel arrives, and everything about the kernel must be proved. This section follows that split (Figure 3): a Lean model of the kernel we can trust, fixed once per target language (Section 4.1); the way from the model to a proof, written by agents and checked by Lean (Sections 4.2 and 4.2); and the short, fixed list of what is left to trust (Section 4.3).

4.1 A Model We Can Trust

In this section, we describe how, ahead of time, a Lean semantic model can be generated for each operation in a target language such as PTX or HIP. This process involves three key components: 1) Machine model: Defining a machine model encompassing memory, register abstraction, fault handling, and concurrency, 2) Per-op semantic contextualization: Specifying per-operation semantics that contextualize the machine model for the chosen target language; and 3) Translator: Developing translators to automate kernel semantic composition and support extension to new target languages.

In this setup, the Lean model of a kernel can be trusted because everything it is built from, a machine model, the semantics of each operation, and a translator, is fixed and checked by human experts before the kernel arrives, and none of it is generated by agents.

Machine model. The machine model of Section 3 is a quadruple M=(Σ,ℐ,sem,cut)M=(\Sigma,\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sem},\mathrm{cut}): the states, the operations of the target language, their semantics, and their classification by the synchronization they perform. Each part trades fidelity for tractability, once, for every kernel.

Memory. A state holds the whole launch:

Σ=𝑝𝑐×𝑟𝑒𝑔×𝑚𝑒𝑚g×𝑚𝑒𝑚s×𝑚𝑒𝑚l×𝑔𝑒𝑜𝑚,\Sigma=\mathit{pc}\times\mathit{reg}\times\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{g}}\times\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{s}}\times\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{l}}\times\mathit{geom},

with 𝑝𝑐\mathit{pc} the program counters, 𝑟𝑒𝑔\mathit{reg} the registers, keyed by thread and name, 𝑚𝑒𝑚g\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{g}} the global memory, 𝑚𝑒𝑚s\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{s}} one shared memory per block, 𝑚𝑒𝑚l\mathit{mem}_{\mathrm{l}} one local memory per thread, and 𝑔𝑒𝑜𝑚\mathit{geom} the read-only launch geometry and coordinates. Keeping every thread’s registers in one state makes it immediate that an operation of one thread touches no register of another. Memories are unbounded, so the model cannot detect an access outside the host’s allocations, which is outside the guarantee (Section 3).

Values. Every register and memory cell holds a typed value or is undefined:

𝑉𝑎𝑙={⊥}∪{(τ,x):τ∈𝑇𝑦,x∈𝑃𝑎𝑦𝑙𝑜𝑎𝑑(τ)},\mathit{Val}=\{\bot\}\cup\{(\tau,x):\tau\in\mathit{Ty},\ x\in\mathit{Payload}(\tau)\},

a type tag τ∈𝑇𝑦\tau\in\mathit{Ty} (the set is listed in Appendix A.7) and a payload xx: an exact real, extended with −∞-\infty for running maxima, under a float tag, an integer under an integer tag, a bit under a predicate. Exact arithmetic is a deliberate idealization, stated once as the scope of the guarantee rather than as an assumption about any kernel: LARK does not track numerical error, Equation 1 is equivalence under exact arithmetic, and floating-point behavior is left to testing checks (Section 4.3).

Faults. semt​(i):Σ⇀Σ\mathrm{sem}_{t}(i):\Sigma\rightharpoonup\Sigma is the semantics of operation ii executed by thread tt, which selects the register row and the coordinates. Its undefined cases are the faults: an IEEE result outside ℝ∪{−∞}\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}, a read of the wrong tag or of ⊥\bot, a misaligned vector access, a negative address, an exhausted fuel (defined below), a non-converged cut. A kernel that can fault has no theorem.

Concurrency. Reasoning about every interleaving of thousands of threads is not practical, and machine-learning kernels do not need it: they work in phases separated by barriers, within which no two threads touch the same data. The model makes phases explicit through cut:ℐ→{⊥,coll,warp,block,grid,halt}\mathrm{cut}:\mathcal{I}\to\{\bot,\mathrm{coll},\mathrm{warp},\mathrm{block},\mathrm{grid},\mathrm{halt}\} (Table 1): a barrier is a cut at its level, a return the halt, and a warp-collective operation such as mma a cut of kind coll\mathrm{coll}, where the lanes of the warp meet and the operation executes once over all their registers. A kernel is a sequence K∈ℐ∗K\in\mathcal{I}^{*} with K⁡[p]K[p] the operation at program counter pp; a thread iterates sem\mathrm{sem} and parks at a cut:

stepK,t​(σ)={semt​(K​[p])​(σ)if cut(K[p])=⊥,σotherwise (parked),\mathrm{step}_{K,t}(\sigma)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{sem}_{t}(K[p])(\sigma)&\text{if }\mathrm{cut}(K[p])=\bot,\\ \sigma&\text{otherwise (parked)},\end{cases}

where p=𝑝𝑐t​(σ)p=\mathit{pc}_{t}(\sigma). A launch is a fold over the hierarchy of units, in time and then in parallelism:

runℓ​(σ)=convℓ(runℓ−1(um)∘⋯∘runℓ−1(u1))(σ).\mathrm{run}_{\ell}(\sigma)=\\ \mathrm{conv}_{\ell}\big(\mathrm{run}_{\ell-1}(u_{m})\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{run}_{\ell-1}(u_{1})\big)(\sigma). (2)

Here u1,…,umu_{1},\dots,u_{m} are the units one level down (the lanes of a warp, the warps of a block, the blocks of the grid) making up the unit at level ℓ∈{warp,block,grid}\ell\in\{\mathrm{warp},\mathrm{block},\mathrm{grid}\}, each run to the next cut of level ℓ\ell; convℓ​(f)​(σ)=f⁡(σ)\mathrm{conv}_{\ell}(f)(\sigma)=f(\sigma) if every thread of the unit parks at one program counter in f⁡(σ)f(\sigma), undefined otherwise; and run0\mathrm{run}_{0} iterates step\mathrm{step} to the lane’s next cut. Each level has a fuel κℓ∈ℕ\kappa_{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}, the steps or sub-runs allowed before its next cut; runℓ0\mathrm{run}^{0}_{\ell} is undefined, so running out of fuel is a fault, and κ→\vec{\kappa} is data the run supplies. The theorem requires σ∈dom⁡(rungridκ→)\sigma\in\mathrm{dom}(\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}}).

Per-operation semantics. Each operation op\mathrm{op} has a lower-layer function op^\widehat{\mathrm{op}}, plain mathematics independent of the machine (add^=+\widehat{\mathrm{add}}={+}, max^=max\widehat{\mathrm{max}}=\max on ℝ∪{−∞}\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}, mma^\widehat{\mathrm{mma}} a tile multiply-accumulate), and an upper layer that binds it to the state. Writing an operation as in the kernel, op​d,a1,…,ak\mathrm{op}\ d,a_{1},\dots,a_{k}, with register names dd and aja_{j}, and τj\tau_{j} and τ\tau for the tags the operation names for operand jj and the result, a scalar operation executed by thread tt is

semt​(op​d,a1,…,ak)​(σ)\displaystyle\mathrm{sem}_{t}(\mathrm{op}\ d,a_{1},\dots,a_{k})(\sigma)
=σ[𝑟𝑒𝑔(t,d)↦(τ,op^(x1,…,xk)),𝑝𝑐t↦𝑝𝑐t+1]\displaystyle=\sigma\big[\mathit{reg}(t,d)\mapsto(\tau,\widehat{\mathrm{op}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})),\ \mathit{pc}_{t}\mapsto\mathit{pc}_{t}+1\big]

if 𝑟𝑒𝑔⁡(t,aj)=(τj,xj)\mathit{reg}(t,a_{j})=(\tau_{j},x_{j}) for every jj and (x1,…,xk)∈dom⁡(op^)(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in\mathrm{dom}(\widehat{\mathrm{op}}), and undefined otherwise. Table 1 gives the schema of each kind of operation: the guard that bounds the domain, the update, and the cut. The operations of each language and their lower-layer definitions are generated from one pinned table per language (Figure 3, per-op semantic formalization), and every definition is measured against a real GPU on random operands before use (Appendix A.5).

Translator. The translator is fixed code, not an agent, and it never guesses. It reads the kernel text bb as data, parseL:𝐵𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠⇀ℐ∗\mathrm{parse}_{L}:\mathit{Bytes}\rightharpoonup\mathcal{I}^{*} (CUDA and HIP through a structured tree whose lowering lowerL:𝑇𝑟𝑒𝑒→ℐ∗\mathrm{lower}_{L}:\mathit{Tree}\to\mathcal{I}^{*} is a definition in MM), so the kernel’s fold is rungridκ→\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}} on K=parseL​(b)K=\mathrm{parse}_{L}(b) and nothing of the semantics is generated per kernel. Every reading is checked by a read-back: a formatter fmtL:ℐ∗→𝐵𝑦𝑡𝑒𝑠\mathrm{fmt}_{L}:\mathcal{I}^{*}\to\mathit{Bytes} writes the data back and fmtL​(parseL​(b))=b\mathrm{fmt}_{L}(\mathrm{parse}_{L}(b))=b must hold byte for byte, so what is trusted is the formatter, a quarter the size of the reader (Appendix A.7). An operation or pattern outside ℐ\mathcal{I} or the concurrency model (asynchronous operations, atomics, a NaN literal) is refused by name before any proof is attempted, since we would rather refuse a correct kernel than prove a wrong theorem (Appendix A.9). Finally, the translator prepares the proof with proved lemmas, generated with their proofs and checked by Lean (the race-freedom lemmas of Section 4.2, the lane bridges and program-counter rungs of Equation 2), and scaffolding lemmas, whose statements it generates and whose proofs an agent writes, so they can be false and then simply fail. Two generator hints, the exact constant behind a rounded literal and the expected launch, guide this generation but decide nothing; Lean can check neither, so both are reported as trusted (Section 4.3).

Retargeting. MM splits as Mlaunch∪LM_{\mathrm{launch}}\cup L: a launch part shared by every language and a per-language part LL, which includes its operations with their semantics and cuts, warp width, reader and read-back formatter, collective lane layouts, and lowering (Appendix A.6). We instantiate LARK for PTX, CUDA, and HIP.

4.2 From Model to Proof

The automated Lean proof flow relies on two key checks: ensuring data race freedom and verifying functional equivalence. Data race freedom can be directly verified within Lean (Figure 3 Stage 1); on the other hand, verifying full functional equivalence may pose computational challenges. To address this, we propose a segment-level approach: first, perform a formally verified flat-model segmentation (Figure 3 Stage 2); then, check functional equivalence at the segment level (Figure 3 Stage 3).

Stage 1: Data-race-freedom check. The fold of Equation 2 runs the units of a phase one after another, while the hardware runs them at once. The two agree only for race-free kernels, so race freedom is the first thing LARK proves about a kernel, before any equivalence is attempted. The vocabulary is the fold’s: a phase ϕ\phi at a level is the run between two consecutive cuts of that level, its units uu are the lanes, warps, or blocks that the level folds, and the footprints Wϕ​(u),Rϕ​(u)⊆𝐿𝑜𝑐W_{\phi}(u),R_{\phi}(u)\subseteq\mathit{Loc} are the locations unit uu writes and reads during ϕ\phi, with 𝐿𝑜𝑐\mathit{Loc} the global, shared, and local addresses and the register names of Σ\Sigma.

Obligation 1 (Race freedom).

RF⁡(K)\mathrm{RF}(K): for every phase ϕ\phi and every two distinct units uj,uku_{j},u_{k} of it, Wϕ​(uj)∩Wϕ​(uk)=∅W_{\phi}(u_{j})\cap W_{\phi}(u_{k})=\emptyset and Wϕ​(uj)∩Rϕ​(uk)=∅W_{\phi}(u_{j})\cap R_{\phi}(u_{k})=\emptyset.

A warp-collective step counts as one more unit: it executes once per warp, with a footprint over the registers of every lane and the memory it reads, and it must meet no lane’s footprint within the warp-level phase around its coll\mathrm{coll} cut, since that cut orders execution, not memory. Race freedom is what the fold needs: the actions of race-free units commute and the barrier that ends a phase orders the phases, so every execution from σ\sigma is finite and ends in the fold’s result, ⟦K⟧M​(σ)=rungridκ→​(σ)\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma)=\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}}(\sigma). This is Lipton’s reduction (Lipton, 1975) as it applies to data-race-free GPU kernels (Adve and Hill, 1990; Collingbourne et al., 2013; Betts et al., 2012; Lustig et al., 2019); we rely on it at every level as metatheory, not as a Lean proof (Section 4.3). To discharge the obligation, the translator derives each footprint from the kernel’s addresses and generates the two lemmas of Obligation 1, with proofs, for every phase and pair of units (Appendix A.10); Lean checks them, an agent attempts any lemma whose proof fails, and a kernel with an unproved lemma is rejected. The condition is sufficient, not necessary: a benign race is rejected as readily as a harmful one (Section 5 reports one found in a production kernel), the price of never accepting a racy kernel.

Stage 2: Verified flat-model segmentation. The kernel’s flat model FK=rungridκ→F_{K}=\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}} on KK follows the kernel line by line with a program counter. Built only from the pre-checked parts of Section 4.1 and the kernel’s text, it is trustworthy, and it is one semantics for every language, so CUDA and HIP are lowered to it at no cost in trust. It is not the proof’s view: it talks about single operations and registers where the Torch module talks about tensors, and a direct proof would unfold it operation by operation with no index to induct on. An agent therefore segments the flat model into a segment-level model GKG_{K}, a term of the grammar

G::=\displaystyle G::={} semt​(i)|G;G|for​j<n​do​G​(j)\displaystyle\mathrm{sem}_{t}(i)\mid G;G\mid\mathrm{for}\ j<n\ \mathrm{do}\ G(j)
∣ifpthenGelseG,\displaystyle\mid\mathrm{if}\ p\ \mathrm{then}\ G\ \mathrm{else}\ G,

read as a partial function on states like FKF_{K}: runs of operations become a sequence, repeated runs one body G⁡(j)G(j) under an index, and a loop a for\mathrm{for} over its body. For the GEMM of Figure 2, the inner loop’s twelve program-counter cases of ldmatrix and mma become one body run four times, and the KK-loop sixteen trips over it. GKG_{K} calls the same semt\mathrm{sem}_{t} as the flat model; only indexing and sequencing change, and a for\mathrm{for} can be treated by induction, one iteration at a time.

Verifying the segmentation. The segmentation was written by an agent, so by our own rule it is not trusted; the stage ends with a Lean-checked obligation.

Obligation 2 (Segmentation).

SEG⁡(K)\mathrm{SEG}(K): for every σ\sigma with InI​(σ,x)\mathrm{In}_{I}(\sigma,x), FK​(σ)=GK​(σ)F_{K}(\sigma)=G_{K}(\sigma).

This is an equality of partial functions, both faulting or both reaching the same state, proved phase by phase by induction on the folded indices from the lemmas the translator prepared (Section 4.1). If the segmentation is wrong, SEG⁡(K)\mathrm{SEG}(K) fails, at no cost in trust.

Proof loop. An agent writes a proof, Lean checks it, and the errors go back to the agent; a proof passes only if it compiles without sorry and #print axioms shows only Lean’s standard axioms. When the attempts run out, a separate agent names the cause, a hard proof, a stuck agent, poorly chosen segments, or a wrong kernel, and the loop continues, restarts, redoes the segmentation, or returns the diagnosis to the kernel generator. This analysis only decides what to try next; whether a kernel is accepted, only Lean decides.

Stage 3: Segment-wise verification loop. The same loop now proves the segment-level model against the Torch semantics, the one place where the formalized module enters.

Obligation 3 (Segment-wise equivalence).

EQ⁡(K,S)\mathrm{EQ}(K,S): for every xx and σ\sigma with InI​(σ,x)\mathrm{In}_{I}(\sigma,x), there is a σ′\sigma^{\prime} with GK​(σ)=σ′G_{K}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime} and OutI​(σ′)=⟦S⟧​(x)\mathrm{Out}_{I}(\sigma^{\prime})=\llbracket S\rrbracket(x).

Segment by segment, the agent shows what each phase and each for\mathrm{for} body leaves in the state, and induction carries it across the iterations. Together the obligations give Equation 1, the theorem of Figure 2(b): EQ⁡(K,S)\mathrm{EQ}(K,S) supplies σ′\sigma^{\prime} with GK​(σ)=σ′G_{K}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime} and OutI​(σ′)=⟦S⟧​(x)\mathrm{Out}_{I}(\sigma^{\prime})=\llbracket S\rrbracket(x), SEG⁡(K)\mathrm{SEG}(K) makes it FK​(σ)=σ′F_{K}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}, and Stage 1 makes that ⟦K⟧M​(σ)=σ′\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}.

Statements. The three stages prove a statement that no agent wrote, which is what the soundness claim rests on: a proof of the wrong statement proves nothing. Its premise and extractor are two definitions fixed once in MM, applied to the task’s signature and launch:

InI:=PreM​(𝑠𝑖𝑔,𝑙𝑎𝑢𝑛𝑐ℎ),OutI:=ExtM​(𝑠𝑖𝑔).\mathrm{In}_{I}:=\mathrm{Pre}_{M}(\mathit{sig},\mathit{launch}),\qquad\mathrm{Out}_{I}:=\mathrm{Ext}_{M}(\mathit{sig}).

PreM\mathrm{Pre}_{M} places every input buffer under its layout, keeps buffers apart and aligned, binds every scalar and dimension, and fixes the launch geometry; ExtM\mathrm{Ext}_{M} reads every output buffer under its layout. The signature has one entry per kernel argument, a buffer with its role, element type, shape, and strided layout, or a scalar or dimension bound to the specification or pinned; it is the list the task’s tests launch with, checked against the kernel’s entry point (Appendix A.8). The theorem quantifies over the kernel’s parameters (base addresses, strides, scalars), every state satisfying the premise, and every input, and the premise is proved satisfiable once for every signature, so no statement holds vacuously.

4.3 What We Still Trust

Trust cannot be removed completely. What LARK does is narrow it, from the whole kernel to a short, fixed list, and report the list with every result. A certificate is

𝒞=(ΠM,ΠK,κ→,π),ΠK=(𝑠𝑖𝑔,𝑙𝑎𝑢𝑛𝑐ℎ),\mathcal{C}=(\Pi_{M},\Pi_{K},\vec{\kappa},\pi),\qquad\Pi_{K}=(\mathit{sig},\mathit{launch}),

with the premises Π=ΠM∪ΠK\Pi=\Pi_{M}\cup\Pi_{K} of Section 3, the fuels κ→\vec{\kappa} the fold runs under (data, not premises: exhausting one is a fault the proof rules out), and a Lean-checked proof

π⊢∀p→​σ​x.PreM​(𝑠𝑖𝑔,𝑙𝑎𝑢𝑛𝑐ℎ)​(p→,σ,x)⇒RF⁡(K)∧∃σ′.(rungridκ→​(σ)=σ′∧ExtM​(𝑠𝑖𝑔)​(p→,σ′)=⟦S⟧​(x)),\pi\vdash\ \forall\vec{p}\,\sigma\,x.\ \mathrm{Pre}_{M}(\mathit{sig},\mathit{launch})(\vec{p},\sigma,x)\Rightarrow\mathrm{RF}(K)\ \wedge\\ \exists\sigma^{\prime}.\ \left(\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}\wedge\mathrm{Ext}_{M}(\mathit{sig})(\vec{p},\sigma^{\prime})=\llbracket S\rrbracket(x)\right),

which with the reduction result of Section 4.2 is K≡M,ISK\equiv_{M,I}S. The two parts of Π\Pi differ in what they are and how they are trusted.

ΠM\Pi_{M} is kernel-independent, the statement that MM is faithful to the hardware ℋ\mathcal{H} of Section 3: the idealizations of MM (exact arithmetic as scope, the fold of Equation 2 with the reduction result of Section 4.2), sem\mathrm{sem} as measured against the hardware, the Lean formalization of the Torch module, and Lean itself (full list in Appendix A.13). The Torch formalization is the one agent-written artifact no proof covers: it is written independently of kernels, auditable on its own, and tested ahead of time against the module.

ΠK\Pi_{K} is kernel-specific and small: the signature and the launch, which come from the task, not from the kernel or an agent (Section 4.2). What remains to believe is that they describe the task, which the report states by quoting them.

Floating-point behavior lies outside Π\Pi: no bound |Kfp​(x)−⟦S⟧​(x)|≤ε|K_{\mathrm{fp}}(x)-\llbracket S\rrbracket(x)|\leq\varepsilon is proved for the kernel KfpK_{\mathrm{fp}} as the hardware rounds it, and LARK claims nothing about rounding, overflow, or quantization; a GPU test against the Torch module answers that question, at a tolerance the report states beside the theorem.

Everything else is proved for the kernel at hand or guarded by refusal: RF⁡(K)\mathrm{RF}(K); the absence of faults, convergence, and termination within the fuel, which together are ⟦K⟧M​(σ)↓\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma){\downarrow}; and SEG⁡(K)\mathrm{SEG}(K) and EQ⁡(K,S)\mathrm{EQ}(K,S). A theorem proved once in MM assembles these into π\pi. Each run exports the certificate as a standalone Lean project that re-checks without LARK (Appendix A.12), with a trusted-assumption report: ΠM\Pi_{M} as a fixed list of statements, ΠK\Pi_{K} quoted, the refusals that applied, and the sites where a named constant was read as exact. Trust is placed only where the report says it is.

5 Experiments

We show that LARK verifies most of the kernels a generation harness writes, each model stopping at a fixed rung of proof difficulty (Section 5.1); that a certificate is robust, rejecting single-site mutants (Section 5.2); and that the method holds on production kernels, where it finds a real race (Section 5.3). Ablations of the failure analysis and the segmentation (Section 5.4) and the takeaways (Section 5.5) close the section.

Setup. We evaluate LARK on KernelCraft (Nie et al., 2026), a recent benchmark of GPU kernel-generation tasks, each with a Torch reference module and tests, which gives LARK its specifications and the tests their baseline: the twelve Level 1 tasks, single operators, on PTX, CUDA, and HIP; and five Level 2 tasks, fused operators (FFN, SwiGLU, RoPE, FlashAttention, GQA), on PTX (Table 6). To measure verification alone, one kernel is generated once and pinned for every task and language, and every model verifies the same kernel. The verification agents are four small models on Level 1 (GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6 Luna) and Opus 5.5 on Level 2, with GLM 5.3, the strongest of the four, as the comparison. Each verification runs under a cap on dialogue rounds per proof step and a spending ceiling, both read off preliminary runs (Appendix A.2). Metrics. A verification passes when it ends in a certificate that Lean accepts with its standard axioms only, and the pass rate is the share of tasks that pass; cost is the input and output tokens of the verification. The numeric screen and the latency measurements use an H100 80GB for PTX and CUDA and an MI300X for HIP.

5.1 Verifying Generated Kernels: Difficulty Set by Proof Shape, Not Language

The tasks form a ladder of proof difficulty, and each model climbs to a fixed height. Table 2 gives the pass rates and token costs on Level 1 and Table 3 the results on Level 2 (per-task outcome details in Appendix A.4.1). On all three languages every model proves the elementwise kernels; the two GLM models also prove the row-wise normalizations (GLM 5.3 stops at its spending ceiling on LayerNorm on HIP); only GLM 5.3 proves the tensor-core and convolution kernels; no model proves DepthwiseConv, and BatchMatmul is proved only on HIP, where the pinned kernel runs one 64-lane wavefront per block instead of four warps; and only Opus 5.5 proves the fused Level 2 kernels (pass rate and cost against model size in Appendix A.4.6). Each step up adds a kind of obligation, an induction over a loop, a convergence fact at a cut, a fragment-layout lemma, and a model that cannot close one kind fails every kernel that needs it. The two kernels that stop every model on PTX and CUDA stop them on difficulty alone: no statement is false, no verdict blames the kernel, no construct is refused, and every model stops on the same proof, one warp’s tensor-core loop of 16 or 26 collective steps carried through the lane, warp, and block folds (Appendix A.4.5). Proof cost follows the same shape: over the 116 PTX and CUDA runs it correlates with the length of the compiled program (Spearman 0.61), while the length barely predicts the number of agent turns (0.17), a turn being one proof attempt and its Lean check, so a long kernel costs more per turn, not more attempts (Appendix A.4.4). Every failure is a proof that ran out of rounds or budget, and on PTX and CUDA the two equivalence proofs take over 90% of a run’s tokens (Appendix A.4.3).

The target language matters less than the kernel, and the lower level is not the harder one. Every model proves nearly the same set of kernels on PTX, CUDA, and HIP: the pass rates of a model differ by at most one task across the three languages, and the rung at which it stops is the same on each. The few cells that differ turn on the shape of the proof, not on the language. GEMV is the clearest case: the two GLM models prove it on PTX but not on CUDA, where the theorem is identical and every failure-analysis verdict was “theorem true, proof hard”, but the kernel compiles to ten segments with two block barriers inside the KK-loop against one segment with one barrier on PTX, so the PTX proof is shorter (29 agent turns against 48 for GLM 5.3). The shorter proof does not come from a weaker kernel: the verified PTX kernels are faster than the CUDA ones on half of the Level 1 kernels and within 5% of them on the rest, and 1.8 times faster on GEMV (Appendix A.4.10).

5.2 Robustness: Rejecting Semantics-Breaking Mutants

To test that a certificate is robust, we mutate verified kernels and ask whether LARK can correctly reject them. Table 4 lists the five mutation rules and the results; each mutant is a verified kernel with one change, on ReLU, Softmax, and GEMM in CUDA, PTX, and HIP. We test one semantics-breaking mutant per applicable rule and kernel; ReLU has no barrier, so R3 applies only to Softmax and GEMM. All runs use GLM 5.3 with the numeric screen disabled.

LARK rejects all 42 mutants: 11 at the translator’s static checks, 10 by a refuted race-freedom obligation, 18 by the failure analysis showing that the kernel computes a different function from the specification, and 3 by a statement Lean refuses because the mutant needs a premise the task’s signature does not give (Appendix A.4.11).

5.3 Verifying Production Kernels

We further evaluate LARK on ten production kernels adapted from vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), FlashInfer (Ye et al., 2025), llm.c (Karpathy, 2024), and flash-attention-minimal (Kim, 2024): nine verify, and the tenth is rejected for a data race (Table 5). Each kernel enters the pipeline through small recorded rewrites, most of which reshape the code without changing what it computes; nine of the ten also carry a semantic departure, such as a 64-bit index read as 32 bits, and each theorem is about the kernel with its departures, all listed in Appendix A.14. The five with the simplest shapes, the rejected one among them, ran with GLM 5.3, the five that fuse stages or run several phases with Opus 5.5.

The rejected kernel shows what a certificate catches that random-input tests do not. llmc_softmax_forward reads, in its last pass, a neighbouring output cell that another thread of the same block writes in the same pass, with no barrier between. The value read is discarded, so the race is benign and no test sees it. The translator cannot derive the footprint of the store, so the obligation falls to the agent, which finds a counterexample instead, two threads of one block storing and loading the same cell of out in the same phase, confirmed by the independent second opinion. The kernel is rejected, since the obligation is over footprints, not over whether a value read is used (Appendix A.14).

5.4 Ablations: Failure Analysis and Segmentation

Two parts of LARK are heuristics outside the trust boundary, and the runs show that both earn their place. The failure analysis, an analyst that names a cause after a failed round, a falsity probe, and an independent second analyst, only chooses what the loop tries next. It is cheap, and it never cut off a proof that was going to succeed. Over the Level 1 runs on PTX and CUDA, the Level 2 runs, and the production kernels (Appendix A.4.9), the analysis costs 0.7% to 4.7% of a model’s input tokens and ended ten dialogues before their ceiling, and in the preliminary runs, where it ran without acting, no proof closed after the point where it would have stopped. It is fallible: it called a correct kernel buggy three times, each refuted by the second analyst; in all, the second analyst disputed eleven of the twenty stopping verdicts it reviewed. None of this touches soundness, since a wrong verdict can only end a run early.

On a complicated kernel the segmentation saves more than its own equivalence proof costs. We conducted an ablation that proves the specification directly against the flat model, with no segmentation and no first equivalence, on FlashAttention on PTX with Opus 5.5. The direct proof closed at 220M input tokens over 20 turns, against 120M over 11 for the second equivalence with the segmentation; with the 49M tokens of the segmentation and its equivalence counted, the direct run still used 29% more and crossed a ceiling the default run finished under, because without segments the agent re-proves the same loop body at every program counter (Appendix A.4.8).

5.5 Discussion

The experiments point to three properties of the framework.

1) Automated formal verification keeps pace with generation. GLM 5.3 certifies 10 of the 12 Level-1 kernels on PTX and on HIP (9 on CUDA) and Opus 5.5 every Level-2 kernel with no human in the loop, which shows that agentic formal verification of GPU kernels is feasible, and the cost per proof falls as the models improve.

2) A robust pipeline with soundness guaranteed. Lean supplies the soundness: a certificate exists only when every obligation is proved, so no agent can talk its way to one. LARK is also robust in practice: wrong segmentations and wrong analyst verdicts ended as failed proofs, semantics-breaking mutants are rejected (Section 5.2), and the one production kernel with a race was rejected while the nine correct ones were certified (Section 5.3).

3) A narrowed trust boundary. What a certificate rests on is independent of the kernel: the machine model, the operation semantics measured against the hardware, and the premise and extractor definitions are fixed and checked offline, before any kernel is seen, the specification is formalized once per task and tested, and everything about the kernel itself is proved. LARK is thus a step toward verifiable code generation in the agentic era: the generator stays untrusted, agents write the proofs, and the certificates are sound.

6 Related Work

Kernel generators and benchmarks (Ouyang et al., 2025; Baronio et al., 2026; Nie et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026) judge a kernel correct when its outputs match a reference on test inputs, a check that generated kernels have been shown to exploit (Lange et al., 2025; Woo et al., 2025). Stricter tests (Sarkar, 2026; Shah and Shrestha, 2026) catch more errors, but on every untested input the kernel’s correctness is still assumed. Earlier formal tools either prove only race freedom (Betts et al., 2012) or rely on human proofs for each program (Ferrell et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2026).

Two recent verifiers have been applied to LLM-generated kernels. Volta (Driscoll et al., 2026) decides equivalence between a PTX kernel and a reference PTX kernel over the reals. Its specification is thus itself a low-level kernel that must be correct, its decision procedure is not mechanically verified, and its evaluation checks only the first pair of thread blocks, which covers the full grid only if every block behaves alike. ProofWright (Chatterjee et al., 2026) has LLM agents annotate CUDA kernels for the VerCors verifier (Armborst et al., 2024), which proves memory and thread safety, but proves equivalence only for element-wise kernels with one output per thread, relying on manual preprocessing of kernels and hand-checked LLM annotations.

In both systems, what must be trusted includes assumptions about, or manual work on, the kernel itself. LARK’s trust boundary is instead fixed before any kernel is seen: for each kernel, it proves in Lean equivalence to the task’s Torch module under exact arithmetic, together with race freedom, absence of faults, and termination, or rejects the kernel. Appendix A.1 discusses further related work.

7 Conclusion

We propose LARK, a framework that verifies LLM-generated GPU kernels against their Torch specifications in Lean, with the trust boundary moved off the kernel. It gives generated code the check it lacked: one that keeps pace with generation and means something when it passes. The machine model and the operation semantics are fixed and checked once per target language; everything about the kernel, race freedom above all, is proved per kernel or the kernel is rejected; and agents may write the segmentations and the proofs because Lean checks every line, so a wrong agent output is a failed proof, never a wrong theorem. GLM 5.3 certifies 10 of the 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all five fused Level-2 kernels, and nine of ten adapted production kernels verify. The tenth, a softmax kernel from llm.c, is rejected for a real data race present in the shipped code, a bug invisible to input–output testing because the racing value is discarded, which LARK located from the code alone.

Limitations

LARK’s guarantee is bounded in three ways. Arithmetic is idealized: floats and integers are exact, +∞+\infty and NaN are faults, and the theorem says nothing about rounding, overflow, accumulation order, or the precision of approximate instructions; floating-point behavior is tested, not proved (Section 4.3). Concurrency is phase-structured: blocks that communicate within a phase, benign races, and warps that halt early are rejected. The operation set is the pinned tables: asynchronous operations (TMA, wgmma, mbarrier), atomics, partial masks, bf16, 8-bit types, non-polynomial addresses, and multi-dimensional blocks are refused (Appendix A.9). None of these changes the method; each costs a pinned definition or a lemma emitter, and retargeting to a new language is manual (Appendix A.6).

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Related Works

Kernel generation and test-based checking.

Existing LLM kernel generation across target languages, from CUDA to close-to-metal assembly (Ouyang et al., 2025; Baronio et al., 2026; Nie et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026), checks correctness by comparing a kernel’s outputs with a reference implementation on sampled inputs. Such testing has proved unreliable: kernels that pass KernelBench’s checks have achieved fake speedups of 5050–120×120\times by exploiting the evaluation harness, and excluding the affected tasks reduces the reported aggregate speedup from 3.13×3.13\times to 1.49×1.49\times (Lange et al., 2025). Reward hacking is likewise a central obstacle for generators trained with reinforcement learning (Woo et al., 2025). Stricter test suites, contract-based checks, and metamorphic testing (Sarkar, 2026; Shah and Shrestha, 2026; Xiao et al., 2022) catch more errors, but their results remain empirical: a kernel that passes them has been checked only on the inputs that were tried, and its correctness on every other input is assumed. The kernel therefore remains inside the trust boundary.

Formal verification and equivalence checking.

Translation validation (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000; Lopes et al., 2021), equivalence checking of program transformations (Pouchet et al., 2024), and verified compilers (Leroy, 2009) relate a program to the source from which it was derived. These techniques do not apply directly to LLM-generated kernels, which have no such source and are specified only by a high-level module in a different language. Interactive proofs against a formal ISA semantics (Ferrell et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2026) exclude the kernel from the trust boundary, but require substantial manual effort for each program. Conversely, GPUVerify (Betts et al., 2012) is fully automatic but establishes only the absence of data races and barrier divergence; since it does not relate a kernel to its specification, the kernel’s functional behavior remains within the trust boundary. LARK combines both properties: it is automatic, treats race freedom as one proof obligation among several, and additionally proves that the kernel is equivalent to its specification.

LLM-driven proving and its failure modes.

LLM agents can now write machine-checked proofs (Feng et al., 2026). A checked proof, however, is only as trustworthy as the statement it proves, and statements are where errors concentrate: audits of Lean benchmarks find missing hypotheses, simplified problems, and vacuous theorems (Ammanamanchi et al., 2026), and models asked to annotate a program for verification have been observed to modify the program instead (Banerjee et al., 2026). When the agent that writes the proof also writes the statement, the statement lies inside the trust boundary, and so does the agent. LARK keeps agents out of the per-kernel trust boundary: the theorem is fixed by the task before the kernel is seen, and Lean checks every proof an agent writes, so an agent’s error about the kernel can only cause a proof to fail, never a certificate for the wrong theorem. The one agent-written artifact that remains trusted, the specification formalization, is per task, tested, and reported as such (Section 4.3).

Formal verification of LLM-generated GPU kernels.

Two recent verifiers have been applied to LLM-generated kernels. Volta (Driscoll et al., 2026), a general equivalence checker, uses symbolic execution to decide equivalence between a PTX kernel and a reference PTX kernel over the reals. Its specification is thus itself a low-level kernel that must be correct, its decision procedure is not mechanically verified, and its evaluation checks only the first pair of thread blocks, which covers the full grid only if every block behaves alike. ProofWright (Chatterjee et al., 2026) has LLM agents annotate CUDA kernels for the deductive verifier VerCors (Armborst et al., 2024), which proves memory and thread safety, but proves equivalence only for element-wise kernels with one output per thread, relying on manual preprocessing of each kernel and hand-checked LLM annotations. LARK instead checks the kernel against the task’s Torch module, fixes its trust boundary before any kernel is seen, and proves in Lean equivalence under exact arithmetic, together with race freedom, absence of faults, and termination, or rejects the kernel.

A.2 Experiment Setup Details

Table 6 lists the evaluated tasks by KernelCraft level, Table 7 the round caps and spending ceilings per model, and Table 8 the kernels by the highest cut level of their phase structure.

Preliminary runs.

The round caps of Table 7 were read off preliminary verify-only runs in which every failed round continued the same dialogue, under a cap of 15 rounds, while the failure analyst still ran and recorded what the normal gate would have done. A round closes an obligation when the agent’s proof of that round discharges one of the open lemmas or goals of the equivalence, and the rule is a high percentile of the last closing round, plus one round of margin. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ran GEMM on PTX eight times, none proving the first equivalence, with last closing rounds at 1, 5, 8, 10, 11, 12, 23, and 23; the 75th percentile gives a cap of 16, which GPT-6 Luna and GLM 5.3 Flash, without preliminary runs of their own, take by decision. GLM 5.3 ran GEMM on PTX three times and proved both equivalences each time, with last closing rounds 1, 1, and 3 for the first and 5, 7, and 6 for the second, a cap of 8. Opus 5.5 ran GQA on PTX once and closed the second equivalence in round 9, a cap of 10. The spending ceilings are the amounts at which these runs were stopped. None of these runs is an evaluation cell.

Table 9 gives the configuration of each evaluated task in the notation of KernelCraft; every task runs at the largest of the benchmark’s five configurations.

A.4 Additional Results

Unless a subsection says otherwise, the analyses below are over the PTX and CUDA runs; the HIP runs enter only the per-task table and the latency measurements.

A.4.1 Per-Task Results on Level 1

Table 11 gives, for every model, language, and task, the outcome and the input and output tokens of the verification. A run ends “pass” with a certificate, “budget” at its spending ceiling, and “fail” when the agent gave up or the round cap was hit.

A.4.2 Refusal Census

Over the 116 PTX and CUDA verifications of the three subsets, no correct kernel was refused by scope: every kernel that passed the numeric screen compiled into the model and reached the proof loop. Outcomes on Level 1, per model (proved / budget stop / agent failure out of 24): GLM 5.3 19 / 5 / 0; GLM 5.3 Flash 13 / 7 / 4; GPT-6 Luna 6 / 0 / 18; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 6 / 0 / 18. On Level 2 (PTX): Opus 5.5 5 / 0 / 0; GLM 5.3 1 / 3 / 1. Library: 10 / 0 / 0.

A.4.3 Cost per Stage

Each verification splits into a static part (the translator’s compile and its Lean modules, the certificate), the agent steps (segmentation, statements, the two proofs, reviews, and the diagnosis), and Lean checks inside the proof loop. Table 12 gives the tokens per stage. On Level 1 the two equivalence proofs take 95 to 99% of a run’s tokens (median per model), the diagnosis 0.7 to 4.4%, and the segmentation, statement, and review steps at most 0.3% each; the segmentation proof dominates for the three weaker models, which rarely reach the equivalence proof, and the equivalence proof dominates for GLM 5.3 and on Level 2. The static part takes 36 to 157 seconds per run (maximum 352); Lean inside the loop 18 to 60 minutes per run for the small models and 6 to 8 for Opus 5.5.

A.4.4 Scaling with Kernel Size

Over the 116 PTX and CUDA verifications, the Spearman rank correlation between the compiled program’s length in program counters and the run’s cost in dollars is 0.61; within a model, between length and tokens, it is 0.43 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 0.55 for GPT-6 Luna, 0.64 for GLM 5.3 Flash and Opus 5.5, and 0.70 for GLM 5.3. Figure 4 plots the proven runs; for the three models with at least ten of them, a least-squares fit in log coordinates has slope 1.03 (GLM 5.3), 0.90 (GLM 5.3 Flash), and 0.99 (Opus 5.5), so within a model the tokens grow about linearly with the program’s length, and the lines differ by the model’s token appetite, not by the kernel. Between length and proof turns it is 0.17, rounds 0.20, and between the number of segments and cost 0.17. Proof cost grows with per-block depth, not with the grid.

A.4.5 Why Every Model Fails on BatchMatmul and DepthwiseConv

Read from the 16 failing Level 1 runs on PTX and CUDA (four models, two kernels): no statement is false and no verdict blames the kernel; every analyst verdict but two is “theorem true, proof hard” or “proof loop stuck”. Every model stops on the same proof. Both kernels pin a 128-thread block whose warps run long chains of tensor-core operations, each once per warp: BatchMatmul’s 16-trip KK-loop of ldmatrix and mma makes one warp’s run of a block phase up to 97 sub-phases, and DepthwiseConv runs 26 collective operations back to back. The generated scaffolding stops at the lane: the per-lane bridges and the trip lemmas are given, but composing them into the warp-level fold across the loop and the collective steps is left to the agent, and that is where every stall is. The two weaker models never close the first equivalence; the two GLM models close it and run out of budget on the second, whose proof must carry the whole dataflow through the staged shared buffers and the fragment-layout arithmetic. Two runs ended on a genuine bug in GPT-6 Luna’s own segmentation, caught by the first equivalence as designed. What would move these kernels is a generated warp-level bridge per block phase, so that the part every model fails on becomes generated, checked text. On HIP the pinned BatchMatmul kernel runs one 64-lane wavefront per block, so the warp-level composition that stops every model here is absent, and GLM 5.3 proves it; DepthwiseConv fails on HIP as on the other two languages.

A.4.6 Model Size and Tokens

Taking the active parameter count as a proxy for capability, Figure 5 plots, for the three small models with published sizes, the Level 1 pass rate, the input tokens per proved kernel, and the input tokens per kernel against active parameters, over PTX and CUDA. The pass rate rises with model size, and the larger model is also the cheaper one per proof: the pass rate goes from 25% to 54% to 79%, and a model that can close a proof needs fewer turns to do it, while a model that cannot spends its rounds and stops. Input tokens per proved kernel: GLM 5.3 (40B active) 466M, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (16B) 1,617M, GLM 5.3 Flash (18B) 2,170M, and GPT-6 Luna 3,313M; mean input tokens per kernel, proved or not: 369M, 404M, 1,175M, and 828M. The largest model is the most efficient per proof, by 3.5 and 4.7 times; DeepSeek and GLM 5.3 spend about the same per kernel, but GLM 5.3 turns it into 19 certificates against 6, while GLM 5.3 Flash fails expensively, running 7 of its 11 failures to the ceiling. Output tokens are 0.7 to 2.4% of input for every model, so the input count carries the comparison; the dialogue re-sent each turn, mostly as cache reads, is the cost, not what the model writes. In dollars the order of DeepSeek and GLM 5.3 per proof is reversed ($39 against $73), only because DeepSeek’s tokens are priced lowest. On Level 2 the gap is wider: Opus 5.5 proves every kernel at 107M input tokens per kernel, a quarter of the 374M GLM 5.3 spends per kernel (Table 3).

A.4.7 The Race-Freedom Fallback

The translator’s generated race-freedom lemmas proved on all 40 Level 1 and Level 2 verifications on PTX and CUDA; the agent fallback of Section 4.2 never ran there. On the production kernels it ran on five of ten, where the translator could not name a footprint: vllm_silu_and_mul (8 turns), llmc_softmax_forward (10 turns), fam_flash_attn (2), vllm_fused_qknorm_rope (7, an output address that divides by the block size), and vllm_awq_gemm (6); four were proved, and on llmc_softmax_forward the fallback returned a located race instead of a proof (Appendix A.14). A later run of the same kernel text reuses the stored proof at no cost.

A.4.8 The Flat-Model Ablation

Three kernels were proved directly against the flat model (no segmentation, no segmentation proof) and compared with their default runs; tokens are input / output in millions. FlashAttention, Opus 5.5, PTX: flat 222.5 / 3.06, of which the direct proof 219.6 / 2.99 in three rounds of 20 turns, against 172.5 / 2.77 for the default run, of which the equivalence proof 119.6 / 2.05 in two rounds of 11 turns and the segmentation with its proof 49.1 / 0.64. The direct proof used 84% more input tokens than the equivalence proof and the whole run 29% more than the default run; it also crossed the $140 ceiling the run started with and finished only after it was raised to the Level 2 ceiling of $200, under which the default run had finished. On the two short kernels, ReLU and GEMM with GLM 5.3 on PTX, the direct proof was cheaper than the default run. Caveats: one hard kernel; the model differs between GEMM and FlashAttention; the default runs ran on an earlier code version than the flat runs.
