A.4.10 Latency

Table 14 and Figure 7 give the latency of the verified evaluation kernels against torch eager, torch.compile, and the fastest vendor library, on an H100 for PTX and CUDA and on an MI300X for HIP; every ratio is against baselines measured on the same device, so the targets are not compared with each other. The Level 2 kernels were verified on PTX only, so PTX covers 17 kernels and CUDA and HIP the twelve Level 1 kernels. The verified kernels beat torch eager on every kernel (geometric mean 5.5×\times on PTX, 4.2×\times on CUDA, 4.1×\times on HIP); torch.compile with max-autotune on 14 of 17 on PTX (2.6×\times), 9 of 12 on CUDA (1.9×\times), and 10 of 12 on HIP (2.1×\times); and the fastest vendor library on 11 of the 14 PTX kernels that have one (1.46×\times), 6 of 9 on CUDA (1.37×\times), and 7 of 10 on HIP (1.22×\times). The PTX kernels are faster than the CUDA ones on 6 of the 12 Level 1 kernels, by the most on GEMV (1.8×\times), BatchMatmul (1.8×\times), and DepthwiseConv (1.4×\times); the other six are within 5%. The losses are the launch-bound elementwise kernels (2 to 5% behind torch.compile on the H100); rmsnorm against FlashInfer (1.3×\times) and, on HIP, against torch.compile (1.8×\times) and AITER (1.5×\times); batchmatmul against the vendor batched GEMM (cuBLAS, built on wgmma and TMA, which are outside LARK’s scope, 1.3×\times on PTX and 2.3×\times on CUDA; hipBLASLt 2.0×\times); SwiGLU on PTX against vLLM’s fused MLP (1.05×\times); GEMV on CUDA and HIP against torch.compile (1.9×\times, 2.0×\times), where the PTX version wins; and LayerNorm on HIP against AITER (1.2×\times).

A.4.11 Mutation Results Analysis

Table 15 reports final-run outcomes after corrections to specification premises and output extraction: 11 static rejections, 10 race-freedom failures, 18 kernel-bug diagnoses, and 3 premise rejections; no mutant escapes. Static and race-freedom checks account for 12 of 15 GEMM rejections, while equivalence failure analysis accounts for most ReLU and Softmax rejections.

A.5 Measuring the Per-Operation Semantics against the Hardware

Every lower-layer definition of Section 4.1 is checked against the GPU before it is pinned. For each operation in a language’s table, a harness draws random operands from declared strata (finite values of each width, −∞-\infty where the operation admits it, boundary cases such as zero and powers of two), runs the operation on the GPU in its own operand form, and compares the result with the Lean definition evaluated on the same operands; a disagreement outside the declared idealizations fails the sweep. The sweep makes no LLM calls and is re-run whenever a table changes; its record is pinned with the table, and a run reads the record its table was pinned on, never the newest. The sweep is what turned one wrong definition into a right one: the approximate base-two exponential had been formalized as exe^{x} and is 2x2^{x}. Shuffles and vector accesses are measured per lane and per alignment in the same way, and the lane layouts of the warp-collective operations are recorded from the hardware before they are pinned.

A.6 Retargeting LARK to a New Target Language

Effort.

CUDA support on top of PTX took at most 39 person-days; its written lines (code, tests, and documentation, generated tables apart) are 68,741, of which 35,314 are code. HIP, ported from CUDA, took 21,495 written lines, of which 15,333 are code, about a third of CUDA’s lines and under half of its code. The shared machine model changed by 885 lines added and 655 removed, including one generalization: the warp width became a parameter, 32 for PTX and CUDA and 64 for HIP, whose wavefront has 64 lanes. HIP’s own translator code is largely a copy of CUDA’s, with 91% of its lines identical. CUDA’s own code is 37 files and 14,062 Python lines and HIP’s 30 files and 7,535 lines, against 221 files and 127,988 lines shared across languages; of the machine model’s Lean text, 96% is shared for HIP, 94% for CUDA, and 86% for PTX.

The split in symbols.

What is fixed once splits as M=Mlaunch∪LM=M_{\mathrm{launch}}\cup L. The shared part

Mlaunch=(Σ,run,conv,RF,PreM,ExtM,𝒞)M_{\mathrm{launch}}=(\Sigma,\mathrm{run},\mathrm{conv},\mathrm{RF},\mathrm{Pre}_{M},\mathrm{Ext}_{M},\mathcal{C})

describes a launch for every language: the state, the folds of Equation 2, race freedom RF\mathrm{RF} and its library (Section 4.2), the premise and extractor definitions PreM\mathrm{Pre}_{M} and ExtM\mathrm{Ext}_{M} (Section 4.2), and the certificate 𝒞\mathcal{C} (Section 4.3). The per-language part

L=(ℐ,sem,cut,wL,parseL,fmtL,𝑙𝑎𝑦𝑜𝑢𝑡L,lowerL)L=(\mathcal{I},\mathrm{sem},\mathrm{cut},w_{L},\mathrm{parse}_{L},\mathrm{fmt}_{L},\mathit{layout}_{L},\mathrm{lower}_{L})

is the operation table with its lower-layer definitions, the warp width wLw_{L} (32 for PTX and CUDA, 64 for HIP), the reader and the read-back formatter, the lane layouts of the warp-collective operations, and, for a structured language, the lowering.

Table 16 lists the components of LARK by whether they are shared across target languages or written per language. The split follows one rule: what describes a parallel launch is written once, what describes a language’s operations is written per language. The machine model MM abstracts GPU execution in general, so its state, value representation, cut hierarchy, folds, and convergence rule, the definition of race freedom with the library that discharges it, the premise schemas, the certificate structure with its end-to-end theorem, the premise and extractor definitions over a signature, the agent loop, and the report are one Lean text and one harness shared by every language. A language supplies its operation set ℐ\mathcal{I}, generated from a pinned table whose lower-layer definitions are measured against the hardware (Appendix A.5); its semantics sem\mathrm{sem} and cut classification cut\mathrm{cut}; a parser and printer, so that the byte round trip of Section 4.1 can check every reading; the lane layouts of its warp-collective operations, recorded from the hardware; and, for a structured language, the lowering of source to the operation sequence, which is itself a pinned Lean definition. The translator’s race-freedom layer is one algorithm with a per-language front end that says what an operation’s operands and memory window are. PTX, being unstructured by design, needs no lowering; CUDA and HIP share the structured-tree lowering and differ in their operation tables and collective layouts.

A.7 Harness Details

Grid barrier.

Block-level barriers are single operations with hardware-defined semantics and a cut of their own. A grid-wide barrier is not: in PTX, grid.sync() lowers to atomic counters and spin loops. LARK pins one template of that lowering, which a PTX kernel copies verbatim with its own registers and labels; the translator reads the copy as one grid-barrier pseudo-operation whose body is the identity and whose cut is grid-level, and the printer re-emits the template from the names it read, so the recognition is covered by the byte round trip. What remains trusted is that the template is a barrier under a cooperative launch. In CUDA and HIP the barrier is the one-line this_grid().sync(). Any other spelling is refused.

Value types.

The type tags of Section 4.1 are 𝑇𝑦={f16,f32,f16x2,intw,pred}\mathit{Ty}=\{\mathrm{f16},\mathrm{f32},\mathrm{f16x2},\mathrm{int}_{w},\mathrm{pred}\}: a 16- or 32-bit float with payload in ℝ∪{−∞}\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}, two packed 16-bit floats held as one value, an integer of width ww with payload in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and a predicate. Other formats (bf16, 64-bit floats, packed 8-bit types) are outside the set and refused by name (Appendix A.9). The payload of a float tag is an element of ℝ∪{−∞}\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}, with −∞-\infty admitted because kernels use it as the initial value of a running maximum; of a packed tag a tuple of them; of an integer tag an element of ℤ\mathbb{Z}, the width being part of the tag; of a predicate an element of {0,1}\{0,1\}. Rounding is hard to reason about, which is why arithmetic is exact in MM and floating-point behavior is left to testing (Section 4.3).

Read-back check.

The translator’s reading of a kernel is not verified; each of its outputs is checked instead, in the manner of translation validation (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000): the parsed data is formatted back to text and compared byte for byte with the source, so a wrong reading passes only if the formatter has a compensating defect. The trust therefore moves from the reader to the read-back formatter, which is the smaller and simpler component: for PTX the reader is 1,405 lines against 320 for the formatter, for CUDA 2,313 against 570, with a 217-line helper shared by both. The formatter walks the emitted data, not the reader’s in-memory objects, so what is printed is the data the theorem is about. The formatter is a trusted item and is listed in the report.

Fuel.

Each level of the fold of Equation 2 runs under a fuel: lane steps per sub-phase, sub-phases per block-level phase, block-level phases per grid-level phase, and grid-level phases per launch. The fuels are data a run supplies, and exhausting any of them is a fault, so a fuel too small for the kernel fails the proof rather than weakening the theorem; nothing about loop bounds is trusted or analysed by a trusted component. The translator proposes generous fuels from the source, and the proof carries termination.

Folds and the proof-friendly restatement.

The folds of Equation 2 are pinned once in MM. The agent’s segment-level model restates the kernel’s run in a sequential shape that a proof can induct on; the first equivalence of Section 4.2 proves that this restatement equals the fold, using the verified race freedom of the kernel, and the second relates the restatement to the specification.

Efficiency mechanisms.

Several mechanisms keep the agent–checker loop efficient: the agent can test lemmas in scratch Lean scripts before committing to them; a timed-out check returns the slowest declarations, the lemmas that passed, and any errors raised, so a failure still yields information; progress and delta submissions let the agent resume from a partial proof or patch part of a program instead of re-emitting it; and context compaction drops the oldest dispensable turns and repeated listings while keeping the system prompt, the first turn, and the most recent messages.

Failure analysis.

When a loop exhausts its attempts, an agentic failure analysis diagnoses the cause (a hard proof, an inefficient proving approach or formalization, or a faulty kernel) and acts accordingly: continue the loop, restart it with a fresh dialogue, redo the formalization, or return the diagnosis to the generation side as feedback for a new kernel. The last path closes the generate-and-verify cycle: a kernel that cannot be proved equivalent because it is wrong is sent back with an explanation of why. The pipeline aborts only when the number of analyses or the overall budget reaches its ceiling.

A.8 Premise Schemas

Every theorem statement is computed from the task’s signature: a list with one entry per kernel argument, in entry order. A buffer entry carries its role (input, output, in-place, or scratch), its element type, its shape, and its layout, a strided tensor in PyTorch’s sense, with each stride a literal or a named integer parameter; a scalar entry carries its domain (any real, or positive) or its pinned value; an integer dimension carries its value. The launch is recorded with it: the block pinned or capped at the declared bound, and the grid pinned, capped and one-dimensional, or merely non-empty, the form chosen by data. The signature is generated from the task’s registry, the same list the task’s tests launch the kernel with, and is checked against the kernel’s entry point by position and kind. The fixed premise over a signature states: every input and in-place buffer placed at its base under its layout, with the memory’s type tags set; every pair of distinct buffers byte-separated; every base aligned to its element size and vector width; every scalar bound to the specification’s input, or pinned; every dimension pinned; every runtime stride at least its row length; and the launch geometry. A scratch buffer is separated and aligned, never placed or extracted; an in-place buffer is placed as an input and read as an output. The fixed extractor reads every output and in-place buffer under its layout. Both are defined once in MM; the facts a proof needs (a placement, a separation, a binding) are projection lemmas of the model, instantiated by name for the run. Satisfiability of the premise is one theorem of MM over every signature whose byte spans fit. Layouts out of scope, refused by name: sub-byte and bit-packed elements, indirection through index buffers, and swizzled or blocked global layouts; shared-memory layouts are internal to the kernel and never part of the premise.

Formally, the signature is a list 𝑠𝑖𝑔∈𝐿𝑖𝑠𝑡⁡(𝐴𝑟𝑔)\mathit{sig}\in\mathit{List}(\mathit{Arg}) with one entry per kernel argument,

𝐴𝑟𝑔::=\displaystyle\mathit{Arg}::={} buf⁡(ρ,τ,𝑠ℎ𝑎𝑝𝑒,𝑙𝑎𝑦𝑜𝑢𝑡)\displaystyle\mathrm{buf}(\rho,\tau,\mathit{shape},\mathit{layout})
∣scalar⁡(𝑑𝑜𝑚)∣​scalar​(v)|dim⁡(n)\displaystyle\mid\mathrm{scalar}(\mathit{dom})\mid\mathrm{scalar}(v)\mid\mathrm{dim}(n)

a buffer with role ρ∈{in,out,inout,scratch}\rho\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{out},\mathrm{inout},\mathrm{scratch}\}, element type τ\tau, shape, and strided layout (element i→\vec{i} at 𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒+|τ|​∑kik​sk\mathit{base}+|\tau|\sum_{k}i_{k}s_{k}); a float scalar bound to a specification input of domain 𝑑𝑜𝑚\mathit{dom} or pinned to vv; an integer dimension pinned to nn. The theorem of Section 4.2 quantifies over the kernel’s parameters p→\vec{p} (base addresses, strides, scalars; Equation 1 folds them into σ\sigma), every state satisfying the premise, and every input, and the satisfiability theorem above reads

∀𝑠𝑖𝑔.∀x∈D.∃p→​σ.PreM​(𝑠𝑖𝑔,𝑙𝑎𝑢𝑛𝑐ℎ)​(p→,σ,x),\forall\mathit{sig}.\ \forall x\in D.\ \exists\vec{p}\;\sigma.\ \mathrm{Pre}_{M}(\mathit{sig},\mathit{launch})(\vec{p},\sigma,x),

proved once for every signature, so no statement holds vacuously.

A.9 Unsupported Constructs

The translator refuses, by name and before any proof is attempted: +∞+\infty as a value and NaN in any form (the creation of either is a fault); integer wraparound and integer division or remainder by zero; bit operations other than a literal mask, a literal shift, and the full warp mask; float-to-integer conversions out of range; the .sat, .ftz, and bf16 forms, FP64, and 8-bit types; asynchronous operations (cp.async, mbarrier, TMA, wgmma, tcgen05, cluster barriers); atomics and fences used for communication; partially masked barriers, shuffles, and collectives; a grid barrier spelled other than the pinned template; addresses that are not polynomial in the thread coordinates, loop counters, and parameters; blocks with more than one dimension and grids with more than two; and any operation absent from the pinned table. Approximate instructions (ex2.approx, lg2.approx, rcp.approx, rsqrt.approx) are accepted and read as the exact function, and the tf32 form of mma is accepted as an FP32 carrier; both are declared idealizations listed in the report. The complete list, with the name of each refusal, ships with the code.

A.10 Race-Freedom Lemmas

Race freedom is what the fold of Equation 2 needs because

RF⁡(K)∧rungridκ→​(σ)=σ′⟹⟦K⟧M​(σ)↓∧⟦K⟧M​(σ)=σ′,\mathrm{RF}(K)\wedge\mathrm{run}^{\vec{\kappa}}_{\mathrm{grid}}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime}\\ \Longrightarrow\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma){\downarrow}\wedge\llbracket K\rrbracket_{M}(\sigma)=\sigma^{\prime},

that is, every execution of KK from σ\sigma, under any scheduling, is finite and ends in σ′\sigma^{\prime}: the actions of race-free units commute, and the barrier that ends a phase orders the phases (Lipton’s reduction, Section 4.2). The translator derives each footprint Wϕ​(u)W_{\phi}(u), Rϕ​(u)R_{\phi}(u) of Section 4.2 as a region polynomial in the thread coordinates, loop counters, and kernel parameters, and generates the two disjointness lemmas of the race-freedom obligation for every phase and pair of units, with proofs over the theorem’s premises, which Lean checks. Where an address is not polynomial in these variables (a clamped index, for instance), the translator cannot name the region: it emits the lemma’s statement without a proof and an agent attempts it, with an independent second opinion on a verdict that the statement is false. A kernel with an unproved lemma is rejected, whether from a real race or a region the translator could not name, and a located race is returned as a counterexample naming the two threads and the cell (Section 5). The condition is sufficient, not necessary: it also rejects units that communicate within a phase, such as producer–consumer blocks.

A.11 Generator Hints

A kernel generator may annotate its kernel with three kinds of hint: the regions each thread writes in a phase, which guide the translator’s choice of footprints when it generates the race-freedom lemmas; a mark naming the exact constant behind a rounded literal, which the translator cross-checks against the literal’s bits and which the pinned decoder then reads as the exact value; and the launch it expects, which selects the launch form of the fixed premise and which the numeric test launches with. The first kind decides nothing, since every lemma built from it is checked by Lean and a wrong region fails a proof. The second and third are the two hints Lean cannot check; both appear in the report.

A.12 Certificate Export

Every run exports its certificate as a standalone Lean project: the pinned model text, the kernel as data with its parse, the signature, the fuels, the race-freedom lemmas, the two equivalence proofs, and the end-to-end theorem, together with the output of #print axioms on that theorem. The project builds with the public Lean toolchain and Mathlib and re-checks without any part of LARK, so a certificate can be audited by a checker that shares no code with the one that produced it. The supplementary material contains the project of the GQA kernel.

A.13 The Kernel-Independent Premises

The kernel-independent premises ΠM\Pi_{M} of Section 4.3 are: (i) the idealizations of MM, exact arithmetic as scope and the fold of Equation 2 with the reduction result of Section 4.2; (ii) the per-operation semantics sem\mathrm{sem}, generated from the pinned tables and measured against the hardware (Appendix A.5); (iii) the pinned grid-barrier template; (iv) a table of four named constants, under which a rounded literal a kernel writes for log2⁡e\log_{2}e is read as the exact value, and the approximate instructions read as exact; (v) the Lean formalization of the Torch module; (vi) the premise and extractor definitions PreM\mathrm{Pre}_{M} and ExtM\mathrm{Ext}_{M}; (vii) the read-back formatter (Appendix A.7); (viii) Lean, its three standard axioms, and its toolchain. Item (v) is tested: a Lean metaprogram evaluates the elaborated specification in 64-bit floating point on random inputs against the Torch module, refusing by name any construct it does not recognize, and the result is reported as evidence, not proof.

A.14 Production Kernels

What “adapted” means.

No production kernel is verified byte for byte as upstream ships it. Each adapted kernel is the smallest mechanical rewrite of the upstream kernel into the pipeline’s input form, and every step is recorded as a change with its reason. The rewrites common to most kernels change the form of the code and not what it computes: one non-template extern "C" kernel per file, with the template instantiated as the library launches it and helpers such as warp reductions inlined; one operation per line, for written as while, no ternary; warp reductions written as full-mask shuffle steps; a lane-0 guard on the per-warp shared store that every lane makes with the same value; a declared block size where upstream declares none, since the theorem pins the block; dynamic shared buffers as static arrays of a covering size; cache hints and programmatic-dependent-launch calls dropped; a 2-D block flattened; vector accesses kept where the race-freedom lemmas cover them and otherwise written as loops of scalar accesses.

Departures.

A step that changes upstream’s semantics is marked as a departure, and the theorem is about the kernel with the departure. They are: 64-bit token and stride indices read as 32-bit (exact at the tested shapes; vllm_silu_and_mul, sglang_rmsnorm, vllm_rms_norm); a runtime alignment test dropped, keeping its aligned path (vllm_rms_norm); the positions gather dropped, so the input is the already gathered rows of the cosine and sine cache, and sizes and flags written as literals (vllm_rotary_embedding, vllm_fused_qknorm_rope); vllm_fused_qknorm_rope made out of place, writing Q and K to a new buffer; the number of threads written as the host’s literal and rsqrt.approx replaced by rsqrtf (flashinfer_rmsnorm); FP32 input and output made FP16 storage (llmc_softmax_forward, fam_flash_attn); the running max and sum made per-thread arrays and the output zeroed by the kernel rather than the host, and __expf replaced by expf (fam_flash_attn); the int4 dequantization removed, so the weights are FP16, a single split-KK iteration, and the block decode’s sizes written as literals (vllm_awq_gemm, transcribed into PTX from upstream’s inline assembly). sglang_fused_add_rmsnorm has no departure and is verified in place, with input and residual as in-out buffers. Per kernel, the rewrite steps and, of them, the departures are: vllm_silu_and_mul 6 and 1, sglang_rmsnorm 10 and 1, sglang_fused_add_rmsnorm 9 and 0, vllm_fused_qknorm_rope 11 and 3, vllm_rotary_embedding 6 and 3, vllm_rms_norm 8 and 2, flashinfer_rmsnorm 12 and 2, llmc_softmax_forward 11 and 2, fam_flash_attn 9 and 4, vllm_awq_gemm 10 and 3.

The llm.c race.

softmax_forward_kernel7 computes the softmax of each row in three passes: a maximum, a sum of exponentials, and a normalization that writes the row of out. In the third pass a thread’s unguarded clamped load __half yh = out[a] with a=min⁡(C−1,k)a=\min(C-1,k) reads a cell of out that another thread of the same block stores at out[a] = qh in the same pass, with no barrier between; the loaded value is used only where k<Ck<C, where the clamped address is the thread’s own cell, so on the tested shapes nothing observable depends on the race. What happened in LARK: the translator’s race-freedom layer builds its footprints from accesses whose addresses are polynomials in the thread and loop indices, and the clamped address is not one, so it refuses to emit its lemma raceFree_1 for the output store, without locating the race, and the obligation goes to the agent fallback of Section 4.2, where the race-freedom statement is false. The fallback’s loop with GLM 5.3 ended after 10 turns and 9.8M input tokens with a counterexample rather than a proof: thread 0 of block 0 at the load with k≥C−1k\geq C-1 reads out[50256], and thread 80 of the same block, the unique writer of that cell, stores it at the third pass’s store; the independent second opinion confirmed the race. A second run with a neutral kernel header found a different witness of the same race (a one-block, 32-thread launch the theorem admits) in 7 turns, so the race is found from the code alone, at about a tenth of what a proof of this kernel costs. The kernel of Table 5 is this original text, and its row records the rejection. A one-line rewrite removes the race: upstream reads out[row + min(C-1, k)] unconditionally, and the rewrite reads out[row + k] under the store’s bounds guard if (k < C), so each thread reads only the cell it then writes, with every other line unchanged and the same values on every input; it verified with Opus 5.5 in a separate run.
